title: The Fed Chair Never Loses a Vote: Warsh Talks Against Guidance, but His Body Is Already Paving the Way for Hikes
dek: Posen gives Warsh's Jackson Hole speech a B-, arguing that he talks against forward guidance while actually paving the way for hikes, and predicts the Fed will raise rates 75-100 basis points over the next six months.
why: Posen is one of the few central-bank watchers willing to say ‘fiscal dominance’ out loud; this episode delivers hard judgments on Fed governance risk, Powell's record, and AI's employment impact, at high information density.
who: Macro traders watching the Fed's path, economists studying AI's impact on employment, and policy researchers concerned about central bank independence.
skip: The last two minutes of subscription and Discord promotion can be skipped.

points.h: Warsh never said he would hike, but the whole speech paved the way
points.body: Posen gives Warsh's Jackson Hole speech a B-, but says it could be treated as a B+ given the chaos of the preceding two months. The fourth section of the speech systematically lists reasons inflation could persist or even rise, yet never says ‘therefore we must tighten.’ Posen reads this as deliberate groundwork: if hikes don't follow, the market will suspect he caved to pressure from Trump. Posen himself has argued for hikes for months, because inflation is real. Warsh also made clear a 2% core PCE target and refused to use wage inflation as a forecasting indicator — both mainstream moves.

points.h: Without defining the ‘right speed,’ returning to target is an empty phrase
points.body: What worries Posen most is that Warsh said at the end of the speech that inflation needs to fall in the ‘right direction’ at the ‘right speed,’ without ever defining what the right speed is. Without a speed constraint, ‘returning to target’ is an empty phrase. From his confirmation hearing to two press conferences to the ECB Sintra speech, Warsh has consistently reserved the right to decide at the last minute, refusing to pre-commit to his own observation indicators. This is close to Greenspan's 1999 style, but Greenspan held up through personal ability and control of the committee; once he erred, the entire credibility would collapse with it.

points.h: The Fed chair never loses a vote
points.body: Posen explains the culture of the Fed committee: unlike the ECB, which seeks consensus, the Fed has historically given the chair more power. More critically, there is an unwritten rule — each meeting has only a few dissents, and the chair never loses a vote. When Volcker found he might lose a vote, he simply announced it would be his last meeting. This culture leaves the committee weak at correcting the chair, so Warsh's ‘reserve discretion’ style carries more risk than he imagines.

points.h: Bashing the central bank isn't dangerous; making it help sell Treasuries is
points.body: Posen distinguishes two kinds of political pressure: ordinary central bank bashing is part of the game and can even help the central bank take the blame when necessary. What is truly dangerous is when a president or treasury secretary asks the central bank to help sell government debt — the central bank must then answer: ‘I am here to help you and your successor sell Treasuries,’ and must never manipulate or cheat. Trump's threats to the Fed are far more serious than rhetoric — trying to strip regional Fed presidents of their votes, disrupting staggered terms, changing the mandate, touching the budget — these directly destroy functional independence.

points.h: The most radical reform may be making the central bank talk less
points.body: Posen thinks the communications committee led by Mervyn King is most likely to produce a radical proposal. King himself is a founder of inflation targeting and fan charts, but since retiring he has publicly doubted the central bank's forecasting ability and information supply: too much noise makes markets depend on official guidance, creating moral hazard and bubbles. Peter Fisher agrees, arguing that central bank ‘certainty’ makes markets less risk-sensitive. The two could push for less information disclosure, not more. The ‘hall of mirrors’ metaphor in Warsh's speech already concedes that markets aren't necessarily right.

points.h: Economists who join AI companies lose their independent voice
points.body: Posen argues that economists flocking to AI companies is not unprecedented — it happened in the internet era too — but this time it is more troubling. Companies like Anthropic hire economists partly to design AI transition policy, and these scholars genuinely believe they are doing good. The problem is that once inside, they enter a corporate hierarchy, lose their independent voice and freedom to choose topics, and their views get reasonably discounted by outsiders. Posen's hope is that scholars stay in research institutes, take low-six-figure salaries, and still have public influence.

points.h: AI replacement hasn't happened yet; programmer employment is still growing
points.body: Posen says labor market data doesn't yet show AI replacement — even employment growth for programmers and truck drivers continues. Brynjolfsson's J-curve theory holds that firms need time to reorganize their businesses, and humans and AI will first have a period of collaboration. Garicano's messy jobs theory points out that the jobs most easily automated actually contain a lot of tacit knowledge and human relationships — a truck driver, for instance, doesn't just drive. Large-scale replacement may take about five years, and will show up first as reduced hiring of young people.

points.h: In six months rates will be 75-100 basis points higher than now
points.body: Posen reiterates that his earlier forecast of 4% year-end PCE inflation is coming true, with CPI already above 4% early in the year. The bigger problem is inflation inertia: although energy prices may pull the numbers down slightly over the next month or two, core services inflation is stubborn, with 3/6/12-month moving averages all rising. He expects the Fed to hike in September or December; if it hikes in September it will hike again in December, and in six months the federal funds rate will be 75-100 basis points higher than now, at which point inflation will only begin to truly decline, spending the interim in a 3.5%-4.5% range.
